newsitem.title: CHINA: China hails copyright war, vendors blast policy.
newsitem.headline: China hails copyright war, vendors blast policy.

text.p: Chinese officials on a sweep through Beijing's computer district on Friday hailed progress in their war on copyright piracy, but vendors criticised government policy as helping to create a huge underground market.

Tougher controls over the audio-visual and software markets had drastically reduced the numbers of fake goods on the shelves of Beijing stores in 1997, said Di Ming, deputy director of the Beijing Anti-Pornography Office.
"This year has been better than last year," Di said while on a sweep of stores in Beijing's hi-tech Haidian district.
"We have stepped up regulation of the market and cleaned out a whole batch of pirated audio-video products and laser discs sold underground," Di told reporters.

In what appeared to be a carefully orchestrated inspection, about 30 police and copyright officials searching for pirated goods were welcomed at the doors by the managers of two large stores selling compact discs, laser video discs and software.
The sweep turned up a small number of pirated compact discs at the first shop but nothing illegal at the second, officials said.

Di declined to say what portion of the multimedia market was taken up by illegal products but Western industry analysts have said legal goods account for about half of music sales and just five percent of total software sales.
China also exports much of its production of pirated goods, analysts say, and U.S. firms have called for stricter border controls and tougher action against illegal factories.

China vowed to clamp down on pirates and open wider its cultural markets in a pact last June with the United States that narrowly averted a multi-billion dollar cross-Pacific trade war over violations of intellectual property rights.
Authorities in Beijing this year had so far seized 50,000 fake video and audio tapes and 30,000 electronic publications, and detained many copyright offenders, Di said.
"Last year the largest piracy case we handled involved more than 30,000 video discs at a single hideout," he said. "This year the largest so far has been just 2,000 or 3,000.
"We are in the process of furthering our crackdown," he said.
But some computer vendors blamed government policies aimed at crushing the black market for actually boosting illegal sales by locking out competition through strict licensing rules.

"We are willing to sell legal copies, but we can't because only state-run, large, or joint-venture companies can get licensed to sell software and games," said the manager of one company selling computer hardware.
"It's too difficult to get into this market," he said. "The government should loosen control and pay more attention to checks."
Unable to win an official licence, many computer companies had turned to hawking software illegally under the table or on the streets, he said.

"Pirated goods aren't sold in these kinds of stores," he said, gesturing at the government-approved Beijing City and Electronics Market where Di's sweep turned up no evidence of copyright infringement.
"Without more people competing, there won't be better economic efficiency and prices will stay too high for average Chinese people," the computer vendor said.
